On Slow Reading

Lyla Aune · February 14, 2026 · 8 minute read

I used to measure my reading by books finished. The number was wrong; the number was the point.

For a while I tracked everything in a spreadsheet: pages per day, books per month, year-end totals. It made reading feel like cardio. The longer I kept the spreadsheet, the less I remembered of any particular book — the speed eroded the substance.

So I stopped. Not the reading; only the counting. And the books, in turn, slowed down. A paragraph could now be a kind of room I sat inside.

Three changes

The first change was that I started underlining things — pencil, lightly, the way librarians used to allow. The second was that I let myself reread the same paragraph until it gave up something I hadn't seen the first time. The third was that I began keeping a small notebook for the sentences I wanted to return to. None of these is original. Their combined effect, however, was.

The pleasure of a sentence is not how fast you get through it, but how slowly it lets you stay.

If you have a pen and a paragraph you trust, you have everything you need.

— L.A., somewhere in Oslo
